'''John Whittle Terborgh''' (born April 16, 1936) is a [[James B. Duke Professor]] of Environmental Science at [[Duke University]] and co-director of the Center for Tropical Conservation. He is a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/john-terborgh-u4y5kw/|title=John Terborgh|website=www.nasonline.org|access-date=2017-07-04}}</ref> and for the past thirty-five years, has been actively involved in [[tropical ecology]] and [[conservation biology|conservation]] issues. An authority on [[Bird|avian]] and [[mammal]]ian ecology in [[Neotropical realm|Neotropical forests]], Terborgh has published numerous articles and books on conservation themes. Since 1973, he has operated the [[Cocha Cashu Biological Station]], a tropical ecology [[research station]] in [[Manú National Park]], [[Peru]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=http://www.cairnspost.com.au/news/cairns/indiana-jones-of-ecology-right-at-home-at-jcu-in-cairns/news-story/617c2093de4543c21a22345329f29ecc?nk=ebc7d30ff62ade7d9ac18afac828987a-1499147643|title=Indiana Jones' of ecology right at home at JCU in Cairns|last=Bateman|first=Daniel|date=2015-10-24|work=[[The Cairns Post]]|access-date=2017-07-04}}</ref>

== Research career ==
Raised in [[Arlington, Virginia]], Terborgh graduated from [[Harvard College]] in 1958 and received his PhD in [[plant physiology]] from [[Harvard University]] in 1963. He served on the faculty of the [[University of Maryland]] and then, for 18 years, on the faculty of [[Princeton University]]. In 1989, Terborgh moved to [[Duke University]], where he joined the faculty of the (now) [[Nicholas School of the Environment]] and founded the Duke University Center for Tropical Conservation.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nicholas.duke.edu/people/faculty/terborgh|title=John W. Terborgh {{!}} Nicholas School of the Environment|last=|first=|date=|website=nicholas.duke.edu|language=en|access-date=2017-07-04}}</ref>

One of the defining features of Terborgh's research is field work in relatively difficult to access tropical regions.<ref name=":1" /> Terborgh studied the elevational distributions of tropical birds in New Guinea with college classmate and friend<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Laichas |first=Tom |date=May 2005 |title=A Conversation with Jared Diamond |url=https://worldhistoryconnected.press.uillinois.edu/2.2/laichas.html |journal=World History Connected |volume=2 |issue=2}}</ref> [[Jared Diamond]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Diamond |first1=Jared M. |last2=Terborgh |first2=John W. |date=1967 |title=Observations on Bird Distribution and Feeding Assemblages along the Rio Callaria, Department of Loreto, Peru |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4159616 |journal=The Wilson Bulletin |volume=79 |issue=3 |pages=273–282 |jstor=4159616 |issn=0043-5643}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Terborgh |first1=John |last2=Diamond |first2=Jared M. |date=1970 |title=Niche Overlap in Feeding Assemblages of New Guinea Birds |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4159922 |journal=The Wilson Bulletin |volume=82 |issue=1 |pages=29–52 |jstor=4159922 |issn=0043-5643}}</ref> and in Peru.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Terborgh |first=John |date=1971 |title=Distribution on Environmental Gradients: Theory and a Preliminary Interpretation of Distributional Patterns in the Avifauna of the Cordillera Vilcabamba, Peru |url=https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2307/1934735 |journal=Ecology |language=en |volume=52 |issue=1 |pages=23–40 |doi=10.2307/1934735 |jstor=1934735 |issn=0012-9658|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Terborgh's study of how competition limits bird ranges involved surveying the Cerros del Sira, "a corner of the world so remote that one must travel a full week to obtain even the most trivial supplies".<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Terborgh |first1=John |last2=Weske |first2=John S. |date=1975 |title=The Role of Competition in the Distribution of Andean Birds |url=https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2307/1935491 |journal=Ecology |language=en |volume=56 |issue=3 |pages=562–576 |doi=10.2307/1935491 |jstor=1935491 |issn=0012-9658|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The Acknowledgements of this paper state "[Terborgh]'s life was saved in a grueling ordeal of emergency by the extraordinary exertions of several unnamed Campa Indians and four Peruvian assistants...".

He has served on several boards and advisory committees related to conservation, including the [[Wildlands Network|Wildlands Project]], [[Cultural Survival]], [[The Nature Conservancy]], [[World Wide Fund for Nature|The World Wildlife Fund]] and both the Primate and Ecology Specialist Groups of the [[International Union for Conservation of Nature]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Wildlands Network |url=http://www.twp.org/about-us/board-directors |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150910154942/http://www.twp.org/about-us/board-directors |archive-date=2015-09-10}}</ref>

Terborgh and his work were among several featured in the documentary film, ''[[The Serengeti Rules]]'', which was released in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web |title='The Serengeti Rules': Film Review |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/review/serengeti-rules-1208985 |access-date=2019-06-06 |website=The Hollywood Reporter |language=en}}</ref>

== Major scientific contributions ==

Terborgh's biography for the MacArthur award states: <blockquote>"Terborgh pioneered the field use of experimental analysis techniques in his early work on the altitudinal distribution of neotropical birds and on the role of competition in bird community structure."<ref name=":0" /></blockquote>This work, along with that of Jared Diamond, highlighted the importance of competition in governing the elevational distributions of tropical birds, in contrast to competing ideas at the time that these distributions were largely governed by bird's climate tolerance.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Freeman |first1=Benjamin G. |last2=Strimas-Mackey |first2=Matthew |last3=Miller |first3=Eliot T. |date=2022-07-22 |title=Interspecific competition limits bird species' ranges in tropical mountains |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abl7242 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=377 |issue=6604 |pages=416–420 |doi=10.1126/science.abl7242 |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=MacArthur |first=Robert H. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3NAYEKc--WAC&dq=macarthur+geographical+ecology&pg=PR11 |title=Geographical Ecology: Patterns in the Distribution of Species |date=1984-07-21 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-02382-3 |language=en}}</ref>

Terborgh's work has also highlighted the importance of predators in keeping herbivores in check, thus allowing plants to thrive (known as the 'Green Earth' hypothesis).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Predators Keep The World Green, Ecologists Find |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2006/02/060228091342.htm |access-date=2023-12-22 |website=ScienceDaily |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Terborgh |first1=John |last2=Lopez |first2=Lawrence |last3=Nuñez |first3=Percy |last4=Rao |first4=Madhu |last5=Shahabuddin |first5=Ghazala |last6=Orihuela |first6=Gabriela |last7=Riveros |first7=Mailen |last8=Ascanio |first8=Rafael |last9=Adler |first9=Greg H. |last10=Lambert |first10=Thomas D. |last11=Balbas |first11=Luis |date=2001-11-30 |title=Ecological Meltdown in Predator-Free Forest Fragments |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1064397 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=294 |issue=5548 |pages=1923–1926 |doi=10.1126/science.1064397 |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Awards and honours ==
In June 1992, Terborgh was awarded a [[MacArthur Fellowship]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=John W. Terborgh |url=https://www.macfound.org/fellows/class-of-1992/john-w-terborgh |access-date=2024-10-30 |website=www.macfound.org |language=en}}</ref> in recognition of his distinguished work in tropical ecology, and in April 1996 he was awarded the [[Daniel Giraud Elliot Medal]] from The National Academy of Sciences for his [[research]], and for his book {{cite book
|title=Diversity and the Tropical Rainforest}} In 2005, he was elected Honorary Fellow of the [[Association for Tropical Biology and Conservation]] during the organization's annual meeting held in [[Uberlândia]], Brazil.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.macfound.org/fellows/478/|title=John W. Terborgh — MacArthur Foundation|website=www.macfound.org|language=en|access-date=2017-07-04}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/daniel-giraud-elliot-medal.html|title=Daniel Giraud Elliot Medal|last=National Academy of Sciences|authorlink=National Academy of Sciences|date=|website=www.nasonline.org|access-date=2017-07-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150905085756/http://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/daniel-giraud-elliot-medal.html|archive-date=2015-09-05|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=http://tropicalbiology.org/fellows/|title=ATBC Honorary Fellows|date=2013-07-31|access-date=2017-07-04|language=en-US}}</ref>
